aimTitle: Understand how the principles of website development are used to create effective websites
aimShort: Purpose and principles of websites; planning a website in response to a client brief
board: Pearson BTEC Level 3 National Extended Certificate in IT (AAQ)

topics.name: Planning a website in response to a client brief

checklist.name: Purpose of websites: eCommerce (selling online), providing information, promoting products or services, providing entertainment
Target audience: demographics (age, gender, income, education, location) and user personas (fictional profiles representing typical users)

Page layout: F-shaped pattern (users scan left-to-right, then down — good for text-heavy sites), Z-shaped pattern (scan across the top, diagonal, across the bottom — good for simple hero pages), grid layout, visual hierarchy (ordering elements by importance), grouping elements, separating content
Navigation: fixed/sticky navigation bars, vertical navigation, hamburger menus, logical navigation (predictable structure)
Content: written content (copy), visual content (images, video), calls-to-action (buttons/links that encourage the user to do something)
Design: typography (fonts, readability), colour scheme (colour psychology, brand colours, contrast)

User experience (UX): accessibility (colour contrast, colour combinations, closed captions and transcripts, keyboard-only navigation, breadcrumbs, customisable features), consistency (branding, page layout, design, UI elements), user-friendly (simple, intuitive, engaging, responsive)
Use of motion and movement: micro-interactions (small feedback animations), animation, parallax scrolling, image sliders; every use of motion must have a purpose
Dynamic websites: customised user experience (e.g. personal recommendations), controlled access to content (e.g. member-only areas)
Cross-browser compatibility: reducing discrepancies between browsers; mobile compatibility
Search Engine Optimisation (SEO): techniques to improve ranking in search results
Planning a website in response to a client brief
Establishing the client's requirements: purpose (the problem to be solved, key messages, user motivations and goals), intended audience, technical requirements

Research to identify new ideas: existing websites (analyse competitors), content ideas, available resources, legal and ethical constraints (copyright, data protection, digital accessibility, inclusive and diverse content and representations)
Structuring the website: site map (number of pages, content and features for each page, site navigation between pages)

Legal and ethical constraints in detail: copyright (don't use others' images/text/music without permission — use Creative Commons, royalty-free stock, or your own assets), data protection (UK GDPR — must have a privacy policy, only collect data you need, ask permission, use forms safely), digital accessibility (WCAG 2.2 guidelines — alt text, contrast, keyboard navigation), inclusive and diverse content (represent different groups positively, avoid stereotypes)

mcq.q: Which of these is a common purpose of a website?
mcq.why: Websites commonly exist for eCommerce, to provide information, to promote products/services, or for entertainment â€” all are valid purposes.

mcq.q: What is a user persona?
options: A fictional profile representing a typical user
A type of website security test
mcq.why: A user persona is a made-up but realistic profile of a typical user â€” their age, goals, habits and frustrations â€” used to design for real people.

mcq.q: Which reading pattern do users most commonly follow on text-heavy websites?
mcq.why: Eye-tracking shows users scan in an F-shape: horizontal lines across the top, then down the left edge. Put key info where eyes go first.

mcq.q: Which layout pattern is best suited to a simple homepage with a strong headline and a call to action?
mcq.why: The Z-pattern suits hero pages: the eye moves top-left, then top-right, then diagonally to the bottom-right where the call to action sits.

mcq.q: What is a benefit of a fixed/sticky navigation bar?
options: Navigation is always visible while scrolling
It removes the need for a sitemap
It makes the page load faster
mcq.why: A sticky nav stays visible as the user scrolls, so they can always find their way around without scrolling back to the top.

mcq.q: Which describes 'visual hierarchy' in page design?
options: Making every element the same size
Placing elements in order of importance so users notice key things first
mcq.why: Visual hierarchy uses size, colour, spacing and position to guide the eye from the most to the least important content.

mcq.q: Why is sufficient colour contrast between text and background important?
options: It makes the site look more colourful
It helps users with visual impairments read the content
It is only for aesthetic appeal
mcq.why: Good contrast (WCAG recommends at least 4.5:1 for normal text) makes text readable for everyone, including users with low vision.

mcq.q: Which of these is an accessibility feature?
mcq.why: Accessibility includes keyboard navigation, alt text, transcripts and captions, breadcrumbs, customisable features and more.

mcq.q: What is a micro-interaction?
options: A short feedback animation, like a button changing colour when clicked
mcq.why: Micro-interactions are small animations that give feedback â€” like a button press effect. Every use of motion should have a purpose.

mcq.q: What makes a website 'dynamic'?
options: It changes colours automatically each day
It customises the user experience or controls access to content, often using server-side processing
mcq.why: Dynamic sites serve customised experiences (recommendations, member areas) â€” usually powered by a server and database, not fixed static pages.

mcq.q: Why must a website be tested across different browsers and devices?
options: Because browsers render HTML, CSS and JS with slight differences
To increase the number of users
It is a legal requirement in the UK
mcq.why: Browsers (Chrome, Safari, Firefox, Edge) and devices (phone, tablet, desktop) can render the same code slightly differently, so cross-browser testing catches discrepancies.

mcq.q: Which of these helps with search engine optimisation (SEO)?
options: Using descriptive page titles and meta descriptions
Using only images (no text) on the page
Hiding keywords in the page background
mcq.why: SEO uses keywords, descriptive titles, meta descriptions, headings, alt text and fast, mobile-friendly pages to help search engines rank your site.

mcq.q: Which of these should you establish first when planning from a client brief?
options: The client's requirements: purpose, audience and technical needs
mcq.why: Everything else â€” structure, design, content â€” flows from understanding the purpose, the intended audience and the technical requirements of the brief.

mcq.q: You find a great photo on Google Images for your client's website. What should you do?
options: Use it â€” everything online is free to use
Check the licence and credit the source, or use royalty-free images
Crop it so the owner won't recognise it
Only use it if the site is not making money
mcq.why: Most images are protected by copyright. Check the licence, credit the source, use Creative Commons or royalty-free stock, or create your own assets.

mcq.q: Your site has a form where users enter their email. Under UK GDPR, what must you provide?
options: A privacy policy explaining what you collect and why, plus consent
Nothing â€” small sites are exempt
mcq.why: GDPR applies to any site processing personal data. You must be transparent about what data you collect, why, and get consent where needed.

mcq.q: Which of these is an example of an entertainment website?
options: A streaming service showing films and series
mcq.why: Entertainment sites exist to amuse or engage users â€” streaming, gaming, music and video platforms are classic examples.

mcq.q: What is the main purpose of an eCommerce website?
options: To sell products or services online
To display a company's contact details only
mcq.why: eCommerce sites are built to sell â€” they include product listings, a shopping basket, checkout and payment processing.

mcq.q: Why is it important to identify the target audience before designing a website?
options: So the design, content and tone match what the audience expects
Because all websites must have an audience
To set the price of the website
mcq.why: Knowing the audience (age, interests, technical ability) shapes everything â€” layout, colour, language, features and content.

mcq.q: Which of these is a demographic factor used to define a target audience?
mcq.why: Demographics include age, gender, income, education, location and occupation â€” all used to build a picture of the audience.

mcq.q: What is the purpose of grouping related content together on a page?
options: To make the page load faster
To make the page easier to scan and understand
To reduce the number of images
mcq.why: Grouping related items (e.g. all navigation together, all product cards together) helps users find what they need quickly.

mcq.q: What is a grid layout in web design?
options: A system of columns and rows used to align content consistently
mcq.why: A grid divides the page into columns and rows so elements align neatly â€” the basis of most professional layouts.

mcq.q: What is a hamburger menu?
options: A navigation icon (three lines) that expands a menu, common on mobile
mcq.why: The hamburger icon (â˜°) collapses navigation into a button, saving space on small screens â€” a common responsive pattern.

mcq.q: What is logical navigation?
options: Organising pages in a way that makes sense to the user, matching how they think
mcq.why: Logical navigation groups pages by meaning (e.g. all 'About' pages together) so users can predict where to find things.

mcq.q: What is a call to action (CTA)?
options: A button or link that prompts the user to take a specific action, like 'Buy now'
mcq.why: A CTA guides the user toward a goal â€” 'Sign up', 'Buy now', 'Contact us' â€” and should be visually prominent.

mcq.q: Why is typography important in web design?
options: It affects readability and the overall feel of the site
mcq.why: Font choice, size, spacing and weight affect how easily users read and how professional the site looks.

mcq.q: What is a colour scheme?
options: The set of colours used consistently across a website
mcq.why: A colour scheme is a deliberate palette used for backgrounds, text, buttons and accents to create a consistent brand feel.

mcq.q: What does 'consistency' mean in user experience design?
options: Using the same layout, colours and patterns throughout the site
mcq.why: Consistency means users learn how the site works once and can apply it everywhere â€” reducing confusion and frustration.

mcq.q: Why should a website be 'user-friendly'?
options: So users can achieve their goals easily without frustration
Because it is a legal requirement
To make it harder to use
mcq.why: A user-friendly site is intuitive, fast and accessible, so visitors stay longer and are more likely to return or convert.

mcq.q: Why should motion on a website be used sparingly?
options: Too much motion distracts users and can hurt accessibility and performance
mcq.why: Motion should have a purpose (feedback, guidance). Excessive animation distracts, slows the page and can trigger accessibility issues.

mcq.q: Which of these is an example of dynamic content?
mcq.why: Dynamic content changes based on the user or data â€” recommendations, member dashboards, live scores and search results.

mcq.q: What is cross-browser compatibility?
options: A site that only works in one browser
A website working correctly across different browsers
mcq.why: Cross-browser compatibility means the site renders and functions correctly in Chrome, Safari, Firefox, Edge and others.

mcq.q: What is a meta description?
options: A short summary of a page shown in search results
mcq.why: A meta description is a brief snippet that appears under the page title in search results, helping users decide whether to click.

mcq.q: Why is a mobile-friendly (responsive) website important for SEO?
options: Google prioritises mobile-friendly sites in search rankings
It reduces the number of pages
mcq.why: Google uses mobile-first indexing, so a responsive site ranks better and provides a better experience for mobile users.

mcq.q: What is a client brief?
options: A document describing what the client wants the website to achieve
A type of contract for hosting
mcq.why: The brief sets out the purpose, audience, features, tone and constraints â€” the starting point for all planning.

mcq.q: Which of these is a technical requirement you might establish from a brief?
mcq.why: Technical requirements include hosting, domain, platform, performance, security and compatibility needs.

mcq.q: Why research existing websites before designing a new one?
options: To learn what works well and what to avoid
mcq.why: Researching similar sites reveals best practice, common features and gaps you can improve on â€” evidence for the assignment.

mcq.q: What is copyright?
options: The legal right of the creator to control how their work is used
mcq.why: Copyright protects original work (text, images, music, code). You need permission or a licence to use someone else's work.

mcq.q: What is a Creative Commons licence?
options: A licence that lets creators share their work with certain conditions
mcq.why: Creative Commons licences allow reuse under set conditions (e.g. attribution, non-commercial) â€” a safe source of assets.

mcq.q: Why must a website be accessible to users with disabilities?
options: It is a legal requirement under the Equality Act and improves the experience for everyone
mcq.why: The Equality Act 2010 requires websites to be accessible, and accessibility also benefits all users (e.g. captions, keyboard nav).

mcq.q: Which of these is a purpose of a promotional website?
options: To advertise a product or service and encourage action
mcq.why: Promotional sites market a product/service, using CTAs and persuasive content to drive sales or enquiries.

mcq.q: What is an informational website?
options: A site whose main purpose is to provide facts and details
mcq.why: Informational sites (news, encyclopaedias, company 'about' pages) exist to deliver facts and knowledge.

mcq.q: What is a user journey?
options: The path a user takes through a website to reach a goal
mcq.why: A user journey maps the steps a visitor takes â€” from landing to completing a task â€” helping you spot friction points.

mcq.q: What is whitespace (negative space) in design?
options: The empty space between elements that improves readability and focus
mcq.why: Whitespace gives content room to breathe, making layouts cleaner and easier to scan â€” a key design principle.

mcq.q: What is a breadcrumb?
options: A navigation trail showing the user's location in the site hierarchy
mcq.why: Breadcrumbs (e.g. Home â€º Products â€º Laptops) show where you are and let users jump back up the hierarchy.

mcq.q: What is a hero section?
options: The large prominent area at the top of a homepage with the main headline and CTA
mcq.why: The hero is the first thing users see â€” a big headline, supporting text and a call to action that sets the tone.

mcq.q: What is a logo?
options: A symbol or design that identifies a brand
mcq.why: A logo is a recognisable mark that represents a company â€” a key part of brand identity.

mcq.q: What is a loading time and why does it matter?
options: How long a page takes to load; slow pages frustrate users and hurt SEO
mcq.why: Fast loading improves user experience and search ranking; slow sites lose visitors. Optimise images and code.

mcq.q: What is a static website?
options: A site with fixed content that doesn't change based on the user
mcq.why: Static sites serve the same content to everyone (e.g. a simple brochure site) â€” simpler but less personalised.

mcq.q: What is a keyword?
options: A word or phrase users type into a search engine
mcq.why: Keywords are the terms people search for; using them naturally in titles, headings and content helps SEO.

mcq.q: What is a constraint in a client brief?
options: A limitation or requirement the design must work within (e.g. budget, deadline, brand rules)
mcq.why: Constraints are boundaries â€” budget, time, brand colours, accessibility, legal rules â€” that shape the design.

mcq.q: What is a competitor analysis?
options: Reviewing similar websites to see what they do well and poorly
mcq.why: Analysing competitors reveals best practice, gaps and opportunities â€” strong evidence for the planning task.

mcq.q: What is a privacy policy?
options: A statement explaining what personal data a site collects and how it's used
mcq.why: A privacy policy is required under GDPR to be transparent about data collection, use and user rights.

mcq.q: What is GDPR?
options: The General Data Protection Regulation governing personal data
mcq.why: GDPR is EU/UK law protecting personal data â€” sites must be transparent, get consent and protect user data.

quiz.q: A restaurant chain wants a site where customers can book tables and order food for collection. What is the site's purpose?
quiz.why: Taking orders and bookings makes it eCommerce plus promotion — serving a clear business purpose.

quiz.q: Which layout principle means putting important content where the eye lands first?
quiz.why: Visual hierarchy arranges elements by importance so users notice key content (headlines, CTAs) first.

quiz.q: When is a hamburger menu most appropriate?
options: Mobile-first designs where space is limited
When the site has one page
quiz.why: Hamburger menus hide navigation behind an icon — ideal on small screens where space is tight.

quiz.q: Which colour pair would NOT be acceptable for WCAG colour contrast?
quiz.why: Light grey on white fails contrast guidelines — poor contrast makes text unreadable for many users. Check contrast with tools like WebAIM.

quiz.q: A client brief targets 'teenagers interested in gaming'. Which is the correct demographic approach?
options: Assume every user is the same age
Design for 13-19 year olds with personas for casual and hardcore gamers
quiz.why: Demographics plus personas let you design content, tone and visuals that actually appeal to the target users.

flashcards.back: The eye-tracking reading pattern on text-heavy pages: horizontal scans across the top, then down the left edge, like the letter F. Put key content in the top-left and upper areas.
Reading pattern on simple hero pages: across the top, diagonal, across the bottom (like Z). Good for landing pages with a headline and a call to action in the bottom-right.
Arranging page elements by importance using size, colour, spacing and position so users notice the most important content first.
A fictional but realistic profile of a typical user (age, goals, habits, frustrations) used to design content and features for real people.
An element that prompts the user to act — e.g. 'Buy now', 'Join free', 'Contact us'. Usually a button or link placed prominently.
A small feedback animation triggered by user action (button press, like button). Uses of motion should always have a purpose, not just decoration.
A navigation bar that stays visible while the user scrolls, so navigation is always one click away.
A navigation icon (three stacked lines) that expands a menu — commonly used on mobile to save space.
A navigation trail showing where the user is (e.g. Home > Music > 1970s). Improves orientation and accessibility.
Ensuring the site displays and works consistently across different browsers (Chrome, Safari, Firefox, Edge) and devices.
Search Engine Optimisation — techniques like keywords, descriptive titles, meta descriptions, alt text and fast mobile-friendly pages that improve search engine ranking.
A site that customises the experience or controls access to content, usually powered by a server and database (e.g. member areas, recommendations).
Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, published by the W3C — the international standard for making web content accessible (contrast, keyboard navigation, captions, etc.).
A diagram showing the structure of the website — every page and how they link together. Required evidence for the assignment.
Placing related elements together (grouping) and using white space/lines to separate different content — improves scanability.

criteria.title: Research and planning for the client brief

criteria.text: Undertake research showing adequate understanding of how website development principles are used to meet a specific purpose, using partially relevant examples.
Produce a site map that partially meets the client's requirements.
Undertake research showing good understanding of how the principles are used, with mostly relevant examples.
Produce a site map that mostly meets the client's requirements.
Carry out effective research demonstrating a thorough understanding of the principles and how to comprehensively meet the client's requirements, using pertinent examples.

briefs.title: Retro Film Hub
briefs.scenario: Midnight Picture Show is a small independent cinema that hosts late-night screenings of classic films. They want a website that introduces young adults (17-23) to the films, stars and cultural moments of Hollywood's golden era.
briefs.purpose: To introduce a young adult audience to classic films and encourage them to visit the cinema.
briefs.targetAudience: 17- to 23-year-olds — many will have seen remakes or references to old films but never the originals.
mustIncludes: Three pages
Drop-down menus
Information about classic films (plot summaries, iconic stars, behind-the-scenes facts)
An accordion (e.g. 'Explore by genre or decade' with expandable sections)
External links to relevant websites (e.g. film archive sites, the cinema's ticketing site)
A form to request a specific film be screened
Modal images (click a film poster to view it enlarged)
Video content with controls (trailers — always embed from official sources)
Search functionality to find films
Accessibility features (alt text, high contrast, keyboard navigation, readable fonts)
briefs.typographyHint: Try a bold display font for headings to echo old cinema signage, with a clean sans-serif for body text.
briefs.colourHint: Golden-era Hollywood palette: deep burgundy, cream, gold and black — or teal and burnt orange for a vintage poster feel.

briefs.title: Community Action Charity
briefs.scenario: A non-profit organisation wants a website to create awareness of its activities and encourage teenagers to join as volunteers. It needs to show positive representations of its members and its work in the community.
briefs.purpose: To create awareness of the charity and encourage a teenage audience to get involved.
mustIncludes: Three pages
Information about the organisation (aims, activities, achievements)
Information about an upcoming event, including a map of the location
One member's personal story (with permission)
An email link to contact the organisation
A form to join the organisation
An interactive image slider with captions
A resource section with filter functionality (text, infographics and video resources)
Positive representations of the organisation and its members
Accessibility features
briefs.typographyHint: Friendly, rounded fonts for headings; clean body text. Avoid jargon — write for teenagers.
briefs.colourHint: Bright, energetic palette (e.g. teal, coral, sunshine yellow) with strong contrast for accessibility.

briefs.title: Local Sports & Fitness Club
briefs.scenario: A local multi-sport club wants a website that promotes its teams and fitness sessions. The club wants to grow its membership among 16-25 year olds and needs the site to showcase facilities, timetables and how to join.
briefs.purpose: To promote the club's teams, sessions and facilities and convert visitors into members.
briefs.targetAudience: 16- to 25-year-olds, including students new to the area
mustIncludes: Three pages
Drop-down menus (sports, sessions, membership)
Information about sports and fitness sessions
An accordion (e.g. frequently asked questions)
External links (e.g. national sport governing bodies)
A form to register interest in joining
Modal images (photo gallery with lightbox)
Video content with controls (session highlights)
Search functionality
Accessibility features
briefs.typographyHint: Strong condensed headings for a sporty energy; keep body text highly readable.
briefs.colourHint: High-contrast sport palette (e.g. royal blue and volt/highlighter accents) — check contrast ratios pass WCAG.
